::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Started 2026-10-12** as this project's first specification. Since
2026-10-14 it covers one entry of the [taxonomy](specification.qmd), code
(Section 3.5 there), for the case where an agent wrote it. Nothing is
decided. Section 4 lists the questions to work through before any of this
becomes a procedure.
:::

## 1. Goal

Work out a validation approach for data analysis code written entirely by an
AI agent, so that a result built on that code can be trusted to the same
standard as one built on code a person wrote and a colleague reviewed.

## 2. Out of Scope

- **Not validation of the AI model itself.** The question is whether a given
  analysis is correct, not whether the agent is good in general.
- **Not scoping the project.** Writing the specification before the agent
  builds is covered by
  [Scoping a project using Agentic Engineering Framework](../ai-agentic-engineering-analysis/index.qmd).
  This project starts once there is code to validate.

## 3. The Existing Checklist

The [validation checklist](https://trinitymetrics.com/references/Validation_Checklist.pdf)
(Sander and Stein) has two parts.

- **Planning.** The intended use of the results, the scripts, inputs and
  outputs to validate, a risk assessment (consequences and likelihood of
  mistakes, and where errors are expected), and a validation approach chosen
  to match the risk: unit tests, spot checks, review of code and outputs,
  re-running step by step, or independent reproduction of key results.
- **Checklist.** Reproducibility and readability overall; reading the right
  file and version, handling missing values and column types on import;
  hard-coded constants on modifying data; and on results, a clean run,
  sensible numbers, cross-checks against other outputs, and no stale outputs
  lying around.

## 4. Open Questions

Each question asks whether a step of the checklist still works when the agent
is the author.

1. **Who is the author and who is the reviewer?** The checklist assumes two
   people. If the agent writes the code and Andy reviews it, Andy is the
   only human who has read it. Is a second agent a reviewer, and what does it
   catch that the first missed?
2. **Where are errors most likely?** The risk assessment asks the authors
   where they expect mistakes. An agent makes different mistakes from a
   person: plausible code that runs cleanly and computes the wrong quantity,
   or a silent change to data handling. Which items on the checklist target
   those?
3. **Is code review still the main check?** An agent produces more code than
   can be read line by line. Does the weight move from reading code to
   independent reproduction of key results and checks on outputs?
4. **Can the agent write its own tests?** Tests written by the same agent
   that wrote the code may share its misunderstanding. What has to come from
   the specification or from a person?
5. **What record shows validation happened?** The checklist produces a
   reviewed set of scripts. With an agent, the prompts, the specification and
   the session may also need keeping.

## 5. First Steps

1. Go through the checklist item by item and mark each as unchanged, changed,
   or no longer applicable when an agent writes the code.
2. Collect published guidance on validating AI-generated code, in
   pharmacometrics and in software engineering generally, and start a
   `references.qmd` once there are sources to track.
3. Try the result on one analysis in this repository that an agent wrote.
